strengths: Introduces a well-motivated, technically sound pipeline (GHOST) that decouples MLLM feedback from the diffusion generator via a lightweight learned mapper, enabling efficient (5-7x faster than DASH) optimization directly in CLIP embedding space while avoiding costly backpropagation through the full generation pipeline.

Extensive empirical validation: results across three open-source MLLMs (Qwen2.5-VL, LLaVA-v1.6, GLM-4.1V-Thinking), transferability experiments to five additional models including closed-source GPT-4o and Gemini2.5-Flash, generalization to ObjectNet, and extension to attribute/relation hallucinations beyond object-existence.

Thorough ablation studies (effect of tau, lambda_clip, lambda_reg, noise level, CLIP-sorting, ensemble object detector filtering) that support the robustness of the design choices and give good insight into the method's behavior.

Careful human evaluation protocol (with calibration/training phase, control images) confirming that GHOST images remain largely perceived as object-free (89%/86.3%) and rated comparably natural to the diffusion baseline.

Demonstrates a practical downstream use (LoRA fine-tuning on GHOST images improves POPE/CHAIR scores) positioning the method as both diagnostic and corrective, and provides substantial reproducibility details (hyperparameters, prompts templates, training configs) in the appendix.

Large improvement in discovered hallucination-inducing samples relative to the most comparable prior work (DASH), showing the value of a targeted, model-in-the-loop generation strategy over passive corpus search.
weaknesses: The headline comparison to DASH is somewhat apples-to-oranges: DASH is designed to search a massive real-image corpus for naturally occurring failures, whereas GHOST directly optimizes/generates images for a much smaller candidate pool; while authors acknowledge this, it still anchors much of the quantitative narrative and may overstate the magnitude of the improvement.

GHOST's realism (FID vs. COCO validation, Table 2) is comparable to or worse than baselines (SD v2.1/unCLIP) for two of three models, indicating a realism/semantic-fidelity trade-off that is not deeply analyzed or discussed beyond a brief mention for GLM.

The mitigation experiment (Section 6.2) is explicitly framed as a small "proof-of-concept" with a single model, limited data scale (3,000 samples), and mixed results (captioning BERTScore slightly decreases after fine-tuning), so the corrective value of GHOST is not convincingly demonstrated at scale.

The method requires white-box access to the target MLLM's next-token probabilities for the target answer token, which is a meaningful practical constraint; while transferability results partly address black-box applicability, the core method itself is not black-box.

Success rates, while much higher than DASH, are still modest in absolute terms (roughly 28-32% on COCO/ObjectNet, and highly variable per-class, e.g., 12-57%), and the paper does not compare against other plausible baselines (e.g., simple pixel-space adversarial perturbations, random image edits, or naive prompt-based text-to-image generation with targeted negative prompts) beyond DASH.

Evaluation is restricted to a fixed set of 10 COCO/ObjectNet object classes per experiment; broader coverage of object diversity or more MLLM architectures (beyond the three primary open-source models) would strengthen claims of generality.

The core technical contribution (embedding-space optimization + diffusion conditioning as an adversarial generation strategy) is an incremental extension of existing adversarial-attack and systematic-failure-discovery literature (DASH, AnyAttack, AttackVLM) rather than a fundamentally new paradigm, which somewhat limits novelty.
